q: What is the most common masonry work in Philippine construction?
n: Laying concrete hollow blocks is by far the most common masonry work in Philippine buildings, for walls, partitions and fences. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (masonry).

q: What rebar size is typically used in 8" CHB walls?
n: 8" (200 mm) CHB walls such as firewalls, exterior and retaining walls are commonly reinforced with 12 mm bars. 10 mm bars suit 4" and 6" walls. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (CHB reinforcement).

q: What rebar size is typically used in 4" CHB walls?
n: 4" (100 mm) CHB partitions are typically reinforced with 10 mm bars at about 0.60–0.80 m vertically and every 3 courses horizontally. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (CHB reinforcement).

q: What is the term for a wall finish that allows the concrete hollow block joints to remain visible?
n: Kostura (from Spanish costura, seam) is the Filipino masonry term for a finish that leaves the block joints visible, i.e. struck or tooled joints instead of a full plaster coat (palitada). Source: Filipino construction trade terminology.

q: What masonry wall combines CHB and brick bonded together?
n: A composite wall bonds different masonry units, such as a CHB backup and a brick face, so they act together structurally as one wall. A veneer is only attached and not bonded. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; ACI 530 / TMS 402 (masonry).

q: Why are steel bars placed even in non-load-bearing masonry walls?
n: Even non-bearing CHB walls are reinforced so they hold together and stay connected to the frame when an earthquake shakes them, instead of collapsing out of plane. Source: NSCP 2015 Chapter 7 (masonry, seismic requirements); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which company manufactures and sells CHB ventilation blocks?
n: Allied Concrete Products Inc. is a Philippine manufacturer of CHB, ventilation (decorative) blocks and other precast concrete products. Source: Company product literature; Philippine building supplier listings.

q: What is the most common mortar in Philippine masonry work?
n: Cement-sand mortar (typically 1:3 to 1:4) is the norm for CHB laying and plastering in the Philippines. Lime mortar is rarely used today. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (mortar).

q: Which mortar type is permitted only for non-load-bearing walls?
n: ASTM C270 ranks mortars M, S, N, O and K by strength. Type K is the weakest (about 75 psi) and is limited to non-loadbearing work such as interior partitions. Source: ASTM C270, Standard Specification for Mortar for Unit Masonry.

q: The steel frame connection in Figure A is called a:
n: In a framed connection, clip angles are shop-attached to the beam web and bolted or welded to the column or girder, transferring shear. Figure A shows this. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, Part 10 (simple shear connections).

q: The steel frame connection in Figure B is called a:
n: Figure B is a simple frame connection: a beam end attached by its web only, transferring shear but not moment. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, Part 10.

q: The steel frame connection in Figure C is called a:
n: A coped connection cuts back the beam's top (and sometimes bottom) flange so it clears the supporting girder's flange and the webs can be bolted together. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, Part 9 (coped beams).

q: The steel frame connection in Figure D is called a:
n: In Figure D the beam flanges are coped (cut away) so the beam web frames into the girder at the same top level. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, Part 9 (coped beams).

q: The steel frame connection in Figure E is called a:
n: Figure E is a simple connection: a pinned, shear-only joint that lets the beam end rotate. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, Part 10 (simple shear connections).

q: What is the main advantage of steel deck?
o: It adds reinforcement to the floor
n: Composite steel deck serves as permanent formwork for the slab, so no removable plywood forms or shoring are needed and floors go up faster. Source: Steel Deck Institute (SDI) Manual; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of these has the highest carbon content?
n: Cast iron has about 2–4% carbon, far more than mild steel (under about 0.3%), stainless steel or wrought iron. That is why it is hard and brittle. Source: ASM Metals Handbook; Callister, Materials Science and Engineering.

q: What device adjusts the tension or length of cables and tie rods?
n: A turnbuckle has two opposite-threaded ends in a sleeve. Turning the sleeve shortens or lengthens the assembly, tensioning cables and tie rods. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; rigging hardware references.

q: What are the main top and bottom members of a steel truss called?
n: The chords are the top and bottom members of a truss and carry the main compression and tension. The web members connect them. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; NSCP 2015 Chapter 5.

q: Which steel connection is preferred for assembling steel parking structures quickly?
n: Bolted connections are fast to erect, need no field welding or weather protection and are easy to inspect, so they are preferred for prefabricated steel parking structures. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual; RCSC Specification for Structural Joints.

q: Which steel section is most used for skylight framing?
n: Hollow structural (tubular) sections are neat, torsionally stiff and easy to glaze against, so they are the most used section for skylight framing. Source: AISC Design Guide 24 (HSS connections); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which steel section best suits an exposed roof truss?
n: Tubular (HSS) members look clean, have no ledges to collect dust or water and are easy to paint, so they suit exposed roof trusses. Source: AISC Design Guide 24; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is a major advantage of tubular steel sections?
n: Tubular sections give a clean, uncluttered appearance with no flanges or ledges, a major reason architects choose them for exposed steel. Source: AISC Design Guide 24 (HSS).

q: Which structure typically uses tubular steel for both strength and looks?
n: Exposed long-span canopies and glazed atriums commonly use tubular steel trusses and space frames, combining structural efficiency with a clean look. Source: AISC Design Guide 24; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is a main fabrication challenge with tubular steel trusses?
n: Tube-to-tube truss joints need profiled (fish-mouth) cuts and full-penetration welds all around a closed section, which makes fabrication more demanding. Source: AISC Design Guide 24 (HSS connections).

q: Which is NOT a usual name for a stainless steel finish?
n: Stainless steel finishes are named by process: No. 4 satin or brushed, hairline, No. 8 mirror and bead blast. "Matte" is not a standard designation. Source: ASTM A480 (stainless finishes); stainless steel supplier literature.

q: Which is NOT a characteristic of stainless steel?
n: Stainless steel resists corrosion through its chromium oxide layer (at least 10.5% Cr). It is not galvanized, which means zinc coating of carbon steel. Source: ASTM A240; International Stainless Steel Forum (ISSF).

q: Which stainless steel finish is common for railings?
n: Railings are commonly finished in a glossy (polished or mirror) stainless finish, which is easy to wipe clean and shows fewer fingerprints. Source: Stainless steel fabricator literature; ASTM A480 finishes.

q: Which stainless steel grade is the general-purpose standard?
n: Type 304 (18/8 chromium-nickel) austenitic stainless is the general-purpose standard grade for architecture and kitchens. Source: ASTM A240; ISSF stainless steel grades.

q: Which stainless grade is best for coastal or marine settings?
n: Type 316 adds about 2% molybdenum, which greatly improves resistance to chloride pitting. It is the grade for coastal and marine settings. Source: ASTM A240; ISSF.
